objectives: Define standard electrode potential E° using the standard hydrogen electrode and write cell diagrams
Calculate E°cell, predict the feasibility of redox reactions and explain the limits of such predictions
Relate E°cell to ΔG° and K, and describe the effect of concentration (Nernst equation) and common cells
reviewNotes: Data used: Ar H 1.0, C 12.0, N 14.0, O 16.0, Na 23.0, Mg 24.0, Al 27.0, S 32.0, Cl 35.5, K 39.0, Ca 40.0, Fe 56.0, Cu 63.5, Zn 65.0, Ag 108.0, Ba 137.0; R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹; molar volume 24.0 dm³ at room temperature and pressure; K_w = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.
E° values are standard 298 K values; check against the board's data booklet. The Nernst equation and the link to K may go beyond the syllabus: flagged for the teacher.
Cell types (fuel cells, lead–acid battery) are not covered here.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Standard electrode potential
blocks.md:
A **half-cell** is a metal in contact with a solution of its ions (or an inert electrode with two species in solution). The **standard electrode potential E°** is the emf of a half-cell connected to a **standard hydrogen electrode** (H₂ at 100 kPa, 1 mol dm⁻³ H⁺, platinum, 298 K) under standard conditions (1 mol dm⁻³ for all ions, 298 K): E°(H⁺/H₂) = 0.00 V.

More **positive** E° means the species on the left (the oxidised form) is a stronger **oxidising agent**; more negative means the metal is a stronger reducing agent.

blocks.title: Cells and feasibility
blocks.md:
In a cell, the half-cell with the more negative E° is the **negative electrode** (oxidation, anode), the more positive is the **positive electrode** (reduction, cathode): **E°cell = E°(positive) − E°(negative)**. A reaction is **feasible** if E°cell > 0.

Values at 298 K (V): Mg²⁺/Mg −2.37; Al³⁺/Al −1.66; Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76; Fe²⁺/Fe −0.44; H⁺/H₂ 0.00; Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34; I₂/I⁻ +0.54; Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ +0.77; Ag⁺/Ag +0.80; Br₂/Br⁻ +1.07; Cl₂/Cl⁻ +1.36; Cr₂O₇²⁻/Cr³⁺ +1.33; MnO₄⁻/Mn²⁺ +1.51.

blocks.caption: The zinc–copper cell: zinc is the negative electrode, copper the positive electrode (E°cell = +1.10 V).
blocks.alt: Two beakers with a zinc electrode in zinc sulfate and a copper electrode in copper sulfate joined by a salt bridge and a voltmeter reading 1.10 volts.

blocks.title: Energy, equilibrium and concentration
blocks.md:
**ΔG° = −nFE°cell** (n = moles of electrons in the equation); a positive E°cell means a negative ΔG° (spontaneous). Also **ln K = nFE°/RT**, i.e. at 298 K lg K = nE°/0.0592.

For non-standard concentrations the **Nernst equation** at 298 K gives **E = E° − (0.0592/n) lg Q**, where Q is the reaction quotient (as for K but with the actual concentrations).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Multiplying E° by the stoichiometric coefficients when balancing: E° does **not** change.
- Subtracting the wrong way: positive electrode minus negative electrode.
- Saying 'feasible' means 'fast': a positive E°cell says nothing about the rate (kinetic barrier).
- Applying standard values to non-standard conditions without commenting (e.g. concentrations, temperature).

blocks.title: Example 1 — The Daniell cell
blocks.statement: A cell has a zinc electrode in 1.0 mol dm⁻³ ZnSO₄ and a copper electrode in 1.0 mol dm⁻³ CuSO₄ joined by a salt bridge. Find E°cell and ΔG° (E°: Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V, Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V).
steps: Zinc is more negative, so zinc is the negative electrode (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻) and copper the positive (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu).

blocks.title: Example 2 — Feasibility and Nernst
blocks.statement: Is it feasible for Fe³⁺ to oxidise I⁻ to I₂? What is E for the Zn/Cu cell when [Zn²⁺] = 0.010 mol dm⁻³ and [Cu²⁺] = 1.0 mol dm⁻³?
steps: A lower [Zn²⁺] makes the cell reaction more favourable, so E rises, as Le Chatelier predicts.

lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Chemistry — physical chemistry (to be checked against the official syllabus)

objectives: Write K_p expressions, calculate partial pressures and K_p for gaseous equilibria
Write K_sp expressions and calculate K_sp from solubility and solubility from K_sp
Predict precipitation and explain the common-ion effect
reviewNotes: K_sp(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ is a typical textbook value; values in the board's data booklet may differ slightly.
The bar chart shows 1.34 and 0.00018 (in units of 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³); the second bar is almost invisible by design.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: K_p for gaseous equilibria
blocks.md:
For a gas mixture the **partial pressure** of A is p_A = (mole fraction of A) × p_total. For aA(g) + bB(g) ⇌ cC(g) + dD(g): **K_p = p_C^c p_D^d / (p_A^a p_B^b)** with the units following from the expression (e.g. atm or Pa to a power). K_p depends only on temperature.

Relation to K_c: K_p = K_c (RT)^Δn, with Δn = moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants (SI units).

blocks.title: Solubility product
blocks.md:
For a sparingly soluble salt in equilibrium with its saturated solution, e.g. AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq): **K_sp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻]** (the solid is omitted). For PbI₂: K_sp = [Pb²⁺][I⁻]². If the solubility is s mol dm⁻³: AgCl: K_sp = s²; PbI₂: K_sp = s(2s)² = **4s³**; Mg(OH)₂: 4s³.

A precipitate forms when the **ionic product Q exceeds K_sp**.

blocks.caption: Solubility of AgCl in water and in 0.10 mol dm⁻³ NaCl: the common ion lowers the solubility (values × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³).
blocks.alt: Two bars: a tall one for solubility in pure water and a very short one in sodium chloride solution.

blocks.title: Common-ion effect
blocks.md: Adding a solution that contains one of the ions of the salt (e.g. NaCl to AgCl) shifts the equilibrium to the left (Le Chatelier): the solubility of the salt **decreases**, but K_sp is unchanged. The effect is used to precipitate ions completely (for example in gravimetric analysis) and explains why salts are less soluble in solutions of common ions.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Forgetting to take mole fractions or to use the total pressure when finding partial pressures.
- Using the wrong power: for PbI₂ [I⁻] = 2s and is squared.
- Not accounting for dilution when two solutions are mixed (concentrations are halved when equal volumes are mixed).
- Saying K_sp changes in the presence of a common ion: only the solubility changes.

blocks.title: Example 1 — K_p
blocks.statement: Initially 1.00 mol of N₂O₄ is heated in a vessel at a constant total pressure of 2.0 atm; at equilibrium 30 % has dissociated: N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂. Find K_p.
steps: At equilibrium: N₂O₄ 0.70 mol, NO₂ 0.60 mol, total 1.30 mol.

blocks.title: Example 2 — K_sp and precipitation
blocks.statement: K_sp(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol² dm⁻⁶. Find its solubility in water and in 0.10 mol dm⁻³ NaCl. Will AgCl precipitate if 50 cm³ of 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ AgNO₃ is mixed with 50 cm³ of 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ NaCl?
steps: In water: s = √K_sp = √(1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. In 0.10 M NaCl: [Cl⁻] ≈ 0.10 so s = K_sp/0.10 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ mol dm⁻³ (7000 times smaller).
After mixing, each concentration is halved: [Ag⁺] = [Cl⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³, so Q = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰.

objectives: Calculate the pH of solutions of weak bases and of salts of weak acids (hydrolysis)

reviewNotes: Data used: Ar H 1.0, C 12.0, N 14.0, O 16.0, Na 23.0, Mg 24.0, Al 27.0, S 32.0, Cl 35.5, K 39.0, Ca 40.0, Fe 56.0, Cu 63.5, Zn 65.0, Ag 108.0, Ba 137.0; R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹; molar volume 24.0 dm³ at room temperature and pressure; K_w = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.
K_a = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ (ethanoic acid) and K_b = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ (ammonia) are standard textbook values (they happen to be equal); indicator ranges are approximate.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Weak bases and salts
blocks.md:
For a weak base B + H₂O ⇌ BH⁺ + OH⁻: K_b = [BH⁺][OH⁻]/[B], so [OH⁻] ≈ √(K_b c); then pOH = −lg[OH⁻] and pH = 14 − pOH. For a conjugate pair: **K_a × K_b = K_w**.

The salt of a weak acid and a strong base (CH₃COONa) is **basic** in water because the anion hydrolyses: CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻, with K_b = K_w/K_a. The salt of a strong acid and a weak base (NH₄Cl) is acidic.

blocks.title: Weak acid titrated with strong base
blocks.md: The curve starts at a higher pH than for a strong acid, rises gradually in the **buffer region**, and has a steep rise at the equivalence point, which is above pH 7. At **half-equivalence** (half of the acid neutralised) [HA] = [A⁻], so **pH = pK_a**: a method to measure K_a. After the equivalence point the curve follows that of excess strong base.

blocks.caption: Titration of a weak acid (ethanoic acid) with a strong base: pH = pK_a at half-equivalence (12.5 cm³), pH about 8.7 at equivalence.
blocks.alt: A titration curve beginning near pH 3, rising slowly through the buffer region, steeply at 25 cm³ to about 11 and flattening near 13.

blocks.title: Choosing an indicator
Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using K_a instead of K_b for the salt of a weak acid (the anion acts as a base).
- Forgetting that mixing changes concentrations (the total volume rises).
- Reading pH = 7 at equivalence for a weak acid titration.
- Using the buffer equation at the equivalence point or beyond: there it is a salt solution or excess base.

blocks.title: Example 1 — A salt of a weak acid
blocks.statement: Find the pH of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ sodium ethanoate (K_a(CH₃COOH) = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, K_w = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴).

blocks.title: Example 2 — Titration of ethanoic acid
blocks.statement: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. Find the pH after 12.5 cm³ and at the equivalence point.
steps: 12.5 cm³ is half-equivalence: [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pK_a = 4.74.
pOH = 5.28, so pH = 8.72: phenolphthalein is suitable.

Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Lattice enthalpy and Born–Haber cycles
blocks.md:
The **lattice enthalpy** (of formation) is the enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic solid forms from its gaseous ions: Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) → NaCl(s). It cannot be measured directly; a **Born–Haber cycle** applies Hess's law to: enthalpy of formation, **atomisation** of the elements, **ionisation energy** of the metal, **electron affinity** of the non-metal and the lattice enthalpy.

Lattice enthalpy is more exothermic for ions with a **higher charge** and a **smaller radius** (MgO ≫ NaCl > KCl).

blocks.title: Entropy and free energy
blocks.md:
**Entropy** S (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) measures the dispersal of energy/disorder: gas ≫ liquid > solid; more particles or moles of gas means higher S. **ΔS° = ΣS°(products) − ΣS°(reactants)**.

The reaction is **feasible** if the free energy change **ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°** is negative (ΔS in kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = J/1000). For ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0 the reaction becomes feasible above T = ΔH/ΔS. Also **ΔG° = −RT ln K**.

blocks.caption: Born–Haber cycle for NaCl (enthalpies in kJ mol⁻¹, not to scale).
blocks.alt: A ladder of energy levels from NaCl(s) at minus 411 up to gaseous sodium ions and chlorine atoms at plus 725, with a red arrow for the lattice enthalpy minus 787.

blocks.title: Reading ΔG
blocks.md: ΔG < 0: feasible (spontaneous in the thermodynamic sense; the rate may still be slow). ΔG = 0: equilibrium. A large negative ΔG° means K ≫ 1; a large positive ΔG° means K ≪ 1. A reaction with ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0 is feasible at all temperatures; ΔH > 0 and ΔS < 0 never.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Mixing the units of ΔS (J) and ΔH (kJ) in ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.
- Using °C instead of kelvin.
- Forgetting to multiply atomisation and ionisation steps by the correct number of moles.
- Saying a negative ΔG means the reaction is fast.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Born–Haber for NaCl
blocks.statement: Find the lattice enthalpy of NaCl from: ΔH_f(NaCl) = −411; atomisation of Na +107; first ionisation energy of Na +496; atomisation of ½Cl₂ +122; electron affinity of Cl −349 (all kJ mol⁻¹).
steps: Hess's law: ΔH_f = ΔH_at(Na) + IE(Na) + ΔH_at(Cl) + EA(Cl) + ΔH_latt.
Sum of the first four steps = 107 + 496 + 122 − 349 = +376 kJ mol⁻¹.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Decomposition of limestone
blocks.statement: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g): ΔH_f (kJ mol⁻¹): CaCO₃ −1206.9, CaO −635.1, CO₂ −393.5; S° (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹): CaCO₃ 92.9, CaO 39.7, CO₂ 213.6. Find ΔG° at 298 K and the temperature above which the reaction is feasible.
steps: ΔG°(298) = 178.3 − 298 × 0.1604 = +130.5 kJ mol⁻¹ (not feasible at room temperature).
blocks.answer: ΔG°(298) = +130 kJ mol⁻¹; feasible above about 1110 K
